chapter: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
title: Weird chords borrowed from Ellington's rehearsals
summary: Horace tried unusual harmonies like F sharp over F, spread out so they sound good, having watched Duke distribute dissonant chords that sounded terrific.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Right, when they just automatically know what to do with it. Did you find yourself -- we've talked a little bit about this before, but did you find yourself experimenting with different kinds of harmony changes? Did you look for different kinds of chord sounds or chord progressions?

Yes, especially after I knew the type of men that I would be writing for, you know. I figured they would make this thing sound good, you know, and they were well experienced enough not to overblow the passage, you know. Like if you had a weird chord, if the third man and the fourth would treat their parts, then you'd have pretty good balance, and you could get away with that, see.
Right. When you say weird chord, just as an example, what might have been considered a weird chord in those days?
Well, I stole a little bit of this from -- at Duke's rehearsal. You know, he defied harmony --

And like you would have an F sharp on top of an F, you know, and start on down, hit your A natural and then your C and one of those things, and it actually was a dischord, but when you hit it and spread it out, sounds good. So -- and Duke did this a lot, and I used to look at that guy and listen at him distribute a chord sometimes, you know, two guys in a hurry, you know, just out of his mind. And I would think just that, I said, 'This guy's out of his mind, I don't want to hear (unintelligible) this chord, you know, and, man, --
